transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Recording: cloud-recording link (shared)
Agenda: POC scoping - workload characterization, success criteria, benchmark plan, timelines

Quick summary (auto):
- Goal: validate Redwood Dedicated latency & cost for Nebula's summarization/generation workloads under realistic bursty QPS and token-skew patterns.
- Success criteria discussed: 99th perc latency < 800ms for gen-paths under target concurrency, cost per 1M tokens under target budget, and reproducible benchmark harness.
- Next: share benchmark sheet and traffic samples; schedule bench run.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Park (AE): ok everyone can hear me? testing audio.
[00:05] Maya Chen (CTO): yes, loud and clear. thanks for setting this up.
[00:08] Jordan Park: cool — want to run quick round robin on who's on the call? we'll go quick.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Maya, CTO. we're building an ML-first ops assistant for infra ticket summarization and automated runbooks.
[00:18] Ethan Graves (SRE): Ethan, SRE lead. we run the in prod infra and care about tail latency, burst behavior and cost.
[00:22] Rhea Kapoor: Rhea, ML platform. I own model infra and run benchmarks internally.
[00:25] Oliver Park: Oliver, product, here to align on timelines.
[00:28] Jordan Park: thanks. from Redwood — Priya SE and Luis SE as well, they'll handle the bench specifics.
[00:33] Priya Menon (SE): hey all. quick note — I'm going to ask a lot about token distributions and concurrency percentiles.
[00:37] Jordan Park: ok let's jump into workload shape. Maya, can you summarize your production traffic shape? QPS, concurrency, burst windows?
[00:42] Maya Chen: sure. baseline QPS is low like 2 to 5 rps, but we see concurrency spikes during morning deploy windows up to 120 concurrent requests for a short 5-10 minute window per region. average request size is small for classification / summarization ~80-120 input tokens, outputs vary — summarization avg 200 tokens, some longer runbook generation up to 800 tokens.
[01:05] Ethan Graves: to add — we have a heavy skew: 70% of calls are quick summarizations (short outputs), 20% medium, 10% big generative flows. The tail is what keeps us up at night.
[01:12] Priya Menon: ok that's helpful. curious: do you have percentiles on token counts? p50/p90/p99?
[01:18] Rhea Kapoor: we have histograms but need to scrub PII. I'll extract p50: 120/200, p90: 250/400, p99: 760/1200 roughly for input/output.
[01:29] Luis Ortega: good. for benching we need distributions + example payloads. and sample QPS series over time to simulate bursts.
[01:35] Jordan Park: success criteria — what does Nebula want to prove in this POC?
[01:38] Maya Chen: three things. 1) confirm we can hit our 99th percentile latency SLO for gen and summarize at our expected concurrency and burst patterns. we're targeting 99th < 800ms for short summarization paths and <2s for the heavy runbook generation. 2) validate cost model — not exceed $X per 1M tokens (note: actual number shared in internal sheet). 3) ops constraints — integrate with our VPC/peering and audit-log export for compliance.
[02:05] Jordan Park: got it — we'll map those to Redwood Dedicated configs (pool sizing, autoscale windows, small/large model variants) and to fallback policies.
[02:11] Priya Menon: quick clarity — are you planning to use hosted or private? you mentioned VPC/peering.
[02:15] Maya Chen: we want private VPC peering to start, but flexibility to burst to Redwood hosted if capacity needed. key gate is audit logs and KMS integration.
[02:24] Priya Menon: perfect. for the bench we'll emulate the private deployment topology — latency numbers might add a small network delta vs hosted but we'll call that out.
[02:31] Ethan Graves: good. about concurrency and memory — can you talk about kv cache and memory impact on the models? we use an LLM with long context occasionally (8k).
[02:40] Luis Ortega: sure — if you run longer context (8k) the kv cache grows and memory per process increases; that affects the density per GPU. we'll propose quantization profile + model shard layout so you can fit expected concurrency.
[02:52] Rhea Kapoor: we do push some requests with 8k but it's <1% of volume. majority under 2k.
[02:58] Priya Menon: then for sizing we usually model three classes: short (<=512), medium (512-2k), long (>2k). we need qps per class and token distribution inside each class.
[03:08] Maya Chen: I'll get class splits in the export.

[03:12] Jordan Park: let's talk bench design. Priya?
[03:14] Priya Menon: suggested plan: 1) static sizing bench: feed representative requests at target QPS and concurrency with synthetic load generator, measure p50/p95/p99 token-level latency and throughput. 2) burst test: replay time-series traffic (real or synthetic) for a 30-minute window to observe autoscale behavior, cold starts, and degradation. 3) cost simulation: run steady-state token throughput to model per-token cost and effective ops cost with caching.
[03:39] Oliver Park: when you say cold starts — do you mean model load time or container startup? what's typical?
[03:44] Priya Menon: both. model load time on GPU is usually ~15-60s depending on model/quant. we use warm pool strategies and fast swap. container startup is smaller but real issue is model GPU memory pressure. warm pools avoid a lot of tail latency.
[03:56] Ethan Graves: can Redwood emulate our real traffic shape (variable QPS + bursty spikes) for the bench? We need representative load.
[04:02] Luis Ortega: yes we'll build a load profile from your time-series and run it against a dedicated cluster; recommend we run with both with and without prefix caching to quantify savings.
[04:12] Rhea Kapoor: prefix caching — we rely on a lot of shared prompts, will cache a lot of kv ideally. need numbers on hit-rate sensitivity.
[04:18] Priya Menon: we'll show a delta: no-cache baseline, 30% hit-rate, 60% hit-rate scenarios. you should provide any internal prompts that are shared.

[04:25] Jordan Park: can you share a sample SLA matrix for the POC acceptance?
[04:29] Maya Chen: acceptance: 1) Short summarization p50 < 200ms, p95 < 400ms, p99 < 800ms under steady-state 60 concurrent; 2) Under burst (120 concurrent for 5-10min) p95 <1.2s and degradation must be graceful with fallback to smaller model variant; 3) Cost: keep projected monthly inference cost within 10% of our budget estimate. 4) Integration: VPC peering validated and logs flowing to our SIEM.
[05:02] Priya Menon: that's concrete, thanks. we'll map to test scenarios and mark pass/fail.

[05:07] Jordan Park: timeline — Nebula expects POC to complete within 4 weeks?
[05:11] Oliver Park: ideally 3-4 weeks. security review may add time. we have a compliance window in early August.
[05:17] Jordan Park: proposed timeline: week 1 — traffic export + baseline config; week 2 — bench runs (static + burst); week 3 — follow-up remediation and re-run; week 4 — final report and handoff. any blockers?
[05:28] Maya Chen: main blocker is getting sanitized traffic and internal signoff for data sharing.
[05:33] Rhea Kapoor: also need to confirm KMS integration details; we use CloudKMS and HSM for master keys.
[05:38] Luis Ortega: we have docs for KMS and VPC peering; we'll share a quick checklist.

[05:44] Ethan Graves: a couple of nitty things — what's your autoscale policy granularity? we worry about scale-up being too slow for 5-10 min bursts.
[05:51] Priya Menon: autoscale uses a two-phase policy: immediate burst buffer (short-lived pre-warmed slots) + scale-up based on sustained queue length. buffer handles short spikes (1-10min) and prevents cold starts. we'll size buffer based on your expected spike amplitude.
[06:07] Ethan Graves: nice. and how do you handle fallback when GPU capacity is saturated?
[06:11] Luis Ortega: routing policy lets requests fall back to a cheaper, smaller model variant or to hosted region. you can define tiered fallbacks by latency budget.

[06:19] Rhea Kapoor: for the benchmark we need token-level breakdowns and also to capture memory usage per replica. can you surface that?
[06:25] Priya Menon: yes — we'll record GPU memory, model footprint, per-request kv hit stats, and CPU network metrics.
[06:31] Jordan Park: any legal/procurement questions upfront?
[06:34] Maya Chen: just standard — we'll need a data processing addendum and SOC2 docs.
[06:38] Jordan Park: we'll email SOC2 report and DPA template.

[06:42] Oliver Park: on cost modelling — how do you calculate per-token cost with autoscale and warm pools? we need an apples-to-apples comparison to our current provider.
[06:49] Luis Ortega: good Q. we'll run a cost sim: map GPU instance hours consumed during workload to token throughput observed, include warm pool overhead, and present effective $/1M tokens. we'll also provide sensitivity to cache hit-rate and quantization.
[07:03] Maya Chen: can you put an estimate of effort and seats required on our side? Who from our team needs to be involved during bench runs?
[07:09] Jordan Park: ideally one SRE, one ML platform (Rhea), and product for acceptance window. SRE should help with peering and network measurements. bench runs are mostly handled by Redwood SEs but we request an on-call on the Nebula side during the 2-hour heavy bench.
[07:22] Ethan Graves: ok I can be on-call.

[07:24] Priya Menon: logistics — we'll share a benchmark template and a traffic export script to collect p50/p90/p99 token histograms and time-series. We prefer a 2-week sample but can work with 3 days if that's easier to sanitize.
[07:38] Rhea Kapoor: we'll start with 7 days and push more if needed.

[07:41] Jordan Park: any other constraints — e.g., model licensing or custom model adjustments?
[07:45] Maya Chen: we use an internally fine-tuned open model — license is Apache. we may need an offline container for the private deployment.
[07:52] Luis Ortega: that's fine. we'll support bringing your model artifact; we'll ask for a model package and a small test harness.

[07:58] Priya Menon: for bench design specifics: we'll run three primary scenarios: steady-state short-path (simulate 60 concurrency), burst-surge (simulate 120 concurrency spike for 10 minutes), and long-run generation tail test where a small subset of requests use 8k context to measure memory and queueing effects.
[08:18] Maya Chen: sounds good. do you simulate real user think time or push as fast as possible?
[08:22] Priya Menon: both variants — closed-loop (where clients wait for responses) and open-loop (firehose) to test saturation. We'll present both results.

[08:30] Jordan Park: ok let's capture open items. Rhea, you will send token histograms, class splits, and example payloads.
[08:36] Rhea Kapoor: yes I'll send by Monday (2026-07-20).
[08:39] Jordan Park: Redwood will send benchmark template and suggested load generator (k6 scripts + traffic replay tool) by Friday (2026-07-17).
[08:45] Jordan Park: final question — do you need us to include a privacy-preserving traffic perturbation tool?
[08:49] Maya Chen: yes that would help to avoid manual sanitization.
[08:52] Luis Ortega: we have a small tool that tokenizes and replaces named entities, we can share an OSS script.
[08:57] Oliver Park: perfect. last thing — what's a clear pass/fail for you?
[09:01] Maya Chen: pass if short-path p99 < 800ms and cost delta <10% vs budget. Fallback behavior documented and VPC peering validated. If we fail a single major acceptance (latency or integration), we re-run after remediation.
[09:17] Jordan Park: understood. we'll capture acceptance matrix in the POC doc.

[09:21] Jordan Park: ok we'll wrap. thanks everyone. quick recap of next steps: Redwood sends template & scripts by 7/17; Nebula shares 7 days of traffic by 7/20; schedule bench run week of 7/27. action items in calendar invite.
[09:35] Maya Chen: thanks all.
[09:36] Ethan Graves: thanks.
[09:37] Rhea Kapoor: bye.

End of transcript.
